doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

chapter: Open City and the economics of records
title: The cost of making a big band record
summary: Davis agrees big band records are paid for out of pocket, praises New York's depth of players and says he pays everyone fairly.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: I wrote down a note here saying it must be a luxury to write for players like that who are going to play it so wonderfully. And then I realized that it’s a luxury that you may have to pay for yourself.

That’s a hundred percent accurate. Yes. Yeah, it’s not — to make a big band record you’re really not looking to recoup even a modest amount of your investment in the product itself. Yes. You’re absolutely right. It’s absolutely fantastic to work with musicians of the caliber on “Open City” is and you know there’s so many really stand out excellent players in New York so we always talk about the depth of players here. So you get down to your eighth call trombone player, it’s still going to be really good. As opposed to some cities that could have — all cities have really good players no doubt, but it’s the depth that you don’t really have so much of. So that’s a real plus here in New York being able to just — and I was able to get pretty much — all my first call people were available. And I booked it for the beginning of January which is typically like a little bit slower timeframe. So if I were trying to book it like for right now, the spring or summer, it would be hit and miss in terms of the players. But yes, it’s a very expensive proposition to do it. And I try to make sure everybody gets paid. I would love to be able to pay them more but I think I’ve built a reputation of being fair and trying to be as
generous as I can. But you’re a hundred percent right, you are going to pay for that if you decide to do that project.
